questions.problem: Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=2-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}$ and the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/5e3f9d31bc4cb5687d784097679861644cc55ce667ea1469d0d790bfe879706f.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=2-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-2$ to $y=2.$ 
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}(2-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(2-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot y{|}_{0}^{2}-{\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4(2-0)-(\frac{(2)^{3}}{3}-0) \\  & =8-\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/7808295803d04d2c996ca7d36110f070a60f4491107ad1c831e6fa8ea9f85678.png)

Find the area $A$ of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)$ and the $y$-axis, as shown above.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)} & =1 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(\pi y) & =1 \\ \pi y & =…,-\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},… \\ y & =…,-\frac{3}{4},\frac{1}{4},\frac{5}{4},…\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, we see that we want to find the area between the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-\frac{3}{4}$ to $y=\frac{1}{4}.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-3/4}^{1/4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-3/4}^{1/4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-3/4}^{1/4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)}{\pi }|}_{-3/4}^{1/4}-{\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y)}{\pi }|}_{-3/4}^{1/4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4})]-\frac{1}{\pi }[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{3\pi }{4})] \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})]-\frac{1}{\pi }[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi }-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\pi } \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is

$$
A=|-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi }|=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi }.
$$

questions.problem: Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=9y-{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis for $y\ge 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(9-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/bbcf218e7b6181c861ba4c804357cc53ae6004453914259a9fe98ad5f09ac4d4.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=9y-{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=3.$ 
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(9y-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{3}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =9\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{3}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =9\cdot (\frac{(3)^{2}}{2}-0)-(\frac{(3)^{4}}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{81}{2}-\frac{81}{4} \\  & =\frac{81}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=2{y}^{2}-2$ and the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-2 & =0 \\ 2{y}^{2} & =2 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/a2156d559a715d668f064c91132719d2678ab4af66bf83591fa5687d6e23d95e.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=2{y}^{2}-2$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-1$ to $y=1.$ 
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-4{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}-4\cdot y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(\frac{1}{3}-0)-4(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}-4 \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{8}{3}|=\frac{8}{3}.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) \\ {e}^{y} & =x+1 \\ x & ={e}^{y}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{y}\,{|}_{0}^{1}-y\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(e-1)-(1-0) \\  & =e-1-1 \\  & =e-2\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x-1}+1,$ the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x-1}+1 \\ y-1 & =\sqrt[3]{x-1} \\ (y-1)^{3} & =x-1 \\ x & =(y-1)^{3}+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}+3y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}+3y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-3{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y+3{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-3\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+3\cdot {\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-3(\frac{1}{3}-0)+3(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) \\ {e}^{y} & =3x \\ x & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $x=y^2-4$ and the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4 & =0 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14013903/assets/f2a29faeb9db8e622a21a0e77bea911960a5c64d87a2c900ecd0c0213b2e4bce.png)

We want the area between the curve $x=y^2-4$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=-2$ to $y=2.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}({y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-8{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot {\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-8y{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2(\frac{8}{3}-0)-8(2-0) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}-16 \\  & =-\frac{32}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $\left|-\dfrac{32}{3}\right| = \dfrac{32}{3}.$

Find the area between the curve $y=\sqrt{x+1},$ the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x+1} \\ {y}^{2} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-1 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $\left|-\dfrac{2}{3}\right| = \dfrac{2}{3}.$
